vignette:
She is 25, an African woman who now works long shifts as a nurse, moving quickly through hospital corridors with a practiced steadiness that other people often read as calm. By the time she reaches my office, though, it is clear that the steadiness costs her something. She speaks softly and keeps her shoulders tight, as if bracing against a blow that has not yet come.

She grows up in a city that becomes dangerous in stages. At first there are rumors, then checkpoints, then the sounds of gunfire at a distance that everyone pretends not to hear. She is still a teenager when the fighting moves closer to her neighborhood. She remembers how ordinary life continues in strange fragments: her mother boiling water for tea, children running errands, music from a neighbor's radio-then sudden bursts of panic when shouting erupts outside or vehicles race past. During one period of intense fighting, she and her family shelter inside their home for days at a time, sleeping in their clothes. She learns to tell the difference between small-arms fire and explosions. She learns which corner of the house feels safest. She learns that safety is temporary.

The worst memory comes from an afternoon when she leaves with a relative to get food and medicine. The streets are nearly empty, littered with broken glass and debris. She remembers the silence just before the blast, then the force of it throwing her to the ground. There is smoke, screaming, dust in her mouth. For a moment she cannot hear anything except a sharp ringing. When she lifts her head, she sees people running and one person lying unnaturally still. Her relative is bleeding and shouting her name, but at first she cannot move. What returns to her later, over and over, is not only fear but the helplessness of that frozen second-her body refusing to respond while everything around her becomes chaos.

After that day, the world feels altered. She startles at every loud sound. If a door slams, her heart races before she can think. At night she lies awake, listening for danger, tracking distant noises, unable to surrender to sleep. When she does sleep, she dreams of smoke and scattering crowds and wakes with her chest pounding, unsure for a few seconds where she is. During the day she tries to act normally for her family, but she becomes watchful and irritable. She scans windows, memorizes exits, notices who is standing too long in one place. She avoids the road where the explosion happened, then avoids going out unless she has to. She tells herself this is common sense, not fear.

Eventually she leaves the war zone and resettles elsewhere. From the outside, her life appears to move forward. She trains as a nurse, drawn in part by a wish she cannot fully explain: to be the person who helps when everything falls apart. In the hospital she is competent and compassionate. She knows how to keep her hands steady during an IV insertion, how to speak gently to frightened patients, how to anticipate what a physician will ask for next. Colleagues rely on her. Patients trust her.

But the hospital also pulls her back into old terror in ways she does not expect. The smell of antiseptic mixed with blood can suddenly transport her. The shrill alarm of a monitor sends a jolt through her body so intense that she has to grip the bedside rail. In the emergency department, when several voices rise at once, her thoughts blur and she feels again the confusion of the blast scene. She is ashamed of how hard she works to hide this. If there is a trauma case or a patient with severe injuries, she becomes hyperfocused in the moment, then later finds herself shaking in the medication room, breathing through nausea. She tells coworkers she just skipped lunch.

At home, her partner notices what others do not. She checks locks more than once before bed. She sits facing the door in restaurants. She asks him to text when he arrives anywhere safely, and if he does not respond quickly her mind fills with catastrophic images she knows are unreasonable but cannot dismiss. Some nights he reaches for her in sleep and she jerks awake, disoriented and defensive, then feels guilty when she sees his face. She wants closeness but often feels removed from it, as if part of her remains on alert even in tenderness. When he asks about her past, she gives him fragments, then says she is tired.

She describes feeling split between two selves: the nurse who functions and the woman who is still waiting for the next explosion. She avoids news about conflict yet cannot stop scanning headlines. Crowded places make her chest tighten. Celebrations with fireworks are unbearable; she smiles, excuses herself, and locks herself in a bathroom until the noise stops. She is frustrated by how vivid the memories remain. "I know I am here," she says, "but my body does not always know."

What troubles her most is the persistence of the fear. She has survived, built a career, found love, and crossed enormous distance from the streets where she once ran for cover. Yet ordinary sounds, certain smells, and moments of sudden uncertainty still collapse time. She is tired of living as if danger is always about to enter the room, tired of carrying the war in a body that never fully learned it was over.
